newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's reputation hinges on tax reform - official.
newsitem.headline: Germany's reputation hinges on tax reform - official.

text.p: As German politicians prepare to resume battle over a wide-reaching tax reform proposal next week, a key industrialist on Sunday warned that the nation's reputation hinged on a compromise.

Hans-Olaf Henkel, head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), told German newspaper Bild am Sonntag that Germany would lose some of its international standing if the tax reform plan, seen as essential to investment, were not pushed through.
"Economic recovery is at the door and the key to this door is called tax reductions," Henkel told the newspaper.

But both Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) were not overly optimistic that a solution could be found, preferring to blame each other for failure.

The Social Democrats have blocked Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax package in parliament which forced the plan to be sent to parliament's 32-member mediation committee, drawn equally from the upper and lower houses.
Wolfgang Gerhard, the leader of the junior coalition partner Free Democrats, however warned the government against agreeing to water down Waigel's ambitious tax reform plans.
In German newspaper Welt am Sonntag, Gerhard said the SPD must decide whether it wants to participate in tax reductions or whether it is not in a position to agree to a reform.
"If the latter is the case, as it is indicated to be, then the coalition should not allow its good plans to be watered down."

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine on the other hand told newsmagazine Focus that the CDU and FDP could not agree a concept amongst themselves and that the coalition was not really willing to agree to a plan that would secure investments and jobs.

German magazine Der Spiegel reported in its latest edition that the coalition plans to present a proposal which would raise the mineral oil tax by 10 pfennigs and the value-added tax by one percentage point.
This would enable a timely reduction of the much loathed solidarity surcharge to rebuild east Germany as well as help reduce contributions for unemployment insurance and pensions.
